In this paper, we address the state estimation problem for dynamical systems using human observations expressed in natural language. In particular, to clearly distinguish such observations from conventional physical sensors that directly measure physical quantities, we refer to them collectively as a human sensor. In this section, we first describe the model of the plant system, and then discuss the model of the human sensor.

We collected observation texts from 5050 participants for each water level ratio between 0%0\% and 100%100\% in increments of 2%2\%, resulting in a dataset of 2,4542,454 pairs. Among these, 1,8821,882 pairs were used for training, 205205 for validation, and 289289 for testing. The training and validation sets were used to train the quantized-label classification model in LAPF and an external DNN in EDAPF. The test set was used to implement the language generation process of the true system described in (21b).

This paper presented the LAPF, a particle filter framework that enables the use of general natural language observations by human agents in state estimation. We conducted a comparative experiment between the LAPF and the EDAPF, and the results demonstrated that the LAPF achieved higher estimation accuracy. Furthermore, in the additional experiment under out-of-domain observation texts, the LAPF exhibited smaller degradation in performance than the EDAPF, indicating its higher robustness to domain shifts in observation texts.

Computation of p​(qkj|sk)p(q_{k}^{j}|s_{k}): We propose a quantized-label classification model, illustrated in Fig. 2.

We describe the structure of the quantized-label classification model, illustrated in Fig. 2. We used the Japanese embedding model “sentence-bert-base-ja-mean-tokens-v2”111https://huggingface.co/sonoisa/sentence-bert-base-ja-mean-tokens-v2 as the text encoder, which maps an input text sks_{k} to a text embedding ek∈ℝ768e_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{768}. This embedding is then processed by a neural network consisting of two hidden layers of 128 and 64 units, each followed by a ReLU activation. The final linear layer maps the 64-dimensional representation to a 5-dimensional feature vector ψk∈ℝ5\psi_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{5}, which is converted into a probability distribution over the five quantized labels via a softmax function.

First, a text encoder processes the observation text sks_{k} to produce an embedding ek∈ℝde_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. A text encoder is a machine learning model that maps an input text into a vector representation capturing its semantics and context. Examples include text embedding models or pretrained language models, and the dimensionality dd of the embedding eke_{k} is typically high, ranging from several hundred to several thousand. Second, a neural network maps the embedding eke_{k} to an mm-dimensional feature vector ψk\psi_{k}. Finally, the softmax function applied to ψk\psi_{k} yields the probability distribution p​(qk|sk)p(q_{k}|s_{k}). This model can be trained using supervised learning with a dataset of text-label pairs {si,qi}i=1Nd\{s^{i},q^{i}\}_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{d}}}. Such a dataset can be constructed by conducting questionnaires, as detailed in Subsection 4.2.

Computing the probability distribution p​(qk|sk)p(q_{k}|s_{k}), rather than directly predicting a single label qkq_{k}, has a benefit in handling out-of-domain observation texts sks_{k}. For example, when an observation text sks_{k} contains features not present in the training data, the model outputs a low-confidence distribution instead of a forced high-confidence label, thereby preventing overconfident and incorrect likelihood updates. This idea is inspired by the approach of sitdhipol2025spatial, which focuses on spatial-language expressions. In contrast, we provide a method applicable to general natural language observations.
